# Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI {.unnumbered} Cleaning is where an AI assistant looks most useful and where its mistakes are hardest to see. A cleaning script can run without error, return the right columns and produce plausible values while having treated a missing-value code as a measurement, kept the same animal twice, or dropped a row nobody noticed. None of these raises an error. By the end of this block you will have checks that catch each of these automatically, every time the cleaning runs: a test that fails if any value changed without a log entry, one that fails if a row disappears, one that fails if more values became missing than the codebook explains, and one that fails if the raw data change at all. That is what makes it safe to let an agent write the cleaning script. This block treats cleaning as four artefacts, each with a different owner: | Artefact | Owner | Why | |---|---|---| | Codebook (`docs/codebook.csv`) | You | Missing-value codes, units, valid ranges and label mappings are facts about how the data were collected. They cannot be inferred reliably from the values. | | Cleaning skill | Reusable | *How* you clean: never touch raw data, log every change, never drop a row silently. The same for every dataset. | | Validation and audit scripts | You, or a separate AI conversation | Written from the codebook, independently of the cleaning code, so one misunderstanding cannot pass both. | | Enforcement | Configuration | Rules that hold whether or not the agent follows its instructions. | The codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI. is the hub. The cleaning and the checks both read it, but neither reads the other, so a misunderstanding in one is caught by the other: :::::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="The cleaning pipeline and its owners. The raw data are pinned by a checksum and profiled with R. You write the codebook from the profile and the data provider's note. Two independent branches read the codebook: the AI cleans with the skill, writing scripts/01_clean.R, the clean data and the cleaning and exclusion logs; the validation rules are transcribed from the codebook separately. The tests and the audit then compare the raw data, the clean data and the logs."} ::::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Facts first ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `data/raw/voles_raw.csv`, pinned by a checksum ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} profiled in R ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-plain} `00_profile.R` output ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} plus the provider's note ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} `docs/codebook.csv` ::: ::::::: ::::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Two branches that read the codebook, never each other ::: :::::: {.dia-branches} ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Skill writes and runs `scripts/01_clean.R` ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} writes ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} Clean data, cleaning log, exclusion log ::: ::::: ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} Validation rules in `validate_voles.R`, transcribed from the codebook ::: ::::: :::::: ::::::: ::::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Then compare ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} Tests and audit: raw data unchanged, every row accounted for, every change logged ::: ::::::: ::: {.dia-caption} Independence is the point: one misunderstanding cannot pass both branches. ::: :::::::: You will work on a version of the voles data with errors planted in it. Your instructor holds the answer key, so at the end you can measure what your pipeline caught and what it missed. *⏱ ~54 minutes* :::{.callout-note} **Why not simply ask the AI to clean the data?** In a 2025 study, language models given deliberately polluted tables found missing values in standard formats but struggled with codes such as `-1` (a sentinel valueA number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for “not recorded” or -1 for “run failed”. It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.), rarely detected non-exact duplicates, and did worse as errors increased (Spreafico et al., 2025). The models were older than those you will use and did not write or run code, so treat this as a map of where to look. Those error classes are planted in this block's data. ::: ## The repository layout This is the part of [your workshop repository](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd) that Block 7 uses: ``` .agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md the skill .claude/ ├── settings.json the deny rules, from Block 6 └── skills/clean-with-codebook/ a copy of the skill folder above .gitattributes stops line-ending changes to raw data data/ ├── raw/voles_raw.csv never edited by anyone └── derived/ cleaning outputs and logs docs/ ├── data_note.md the data provider's note ├── profile.csv written by 00_profile.R in Step 1 └── codebook.csv you write this in Step 2 scripts/ ├── 00_profile.R provided ├── 01_clean.R written by the agent in Step 4 ├── 02_validate.R provided: raw should fail, clean pass ├── 03_audit_cleaning.R provided └── functions/validate_voles.R provided tests/ ├── fixtures/raw_checksum.txt you create this in Step 0 ├── test_cleaning.R provided └── test_audit.R provided ``` If your workshop repository does not already contain `.agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/`, download the skill and unzip it into `.agents/skills/`. In the R console, `unzip(file.choose(), exdir = here::here(".agents", "skills"))` lets you pick the downloaded zip: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Claude Code reads skills from `.claude/skills/`, so copy the folder there as well. In the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fs::dir_copy( here::here(".agents", "skills", "clean-with-codebook"), here::here(".claude", "skills", "clean-with-codebook"), overwrite = TRUE ) ``` ::: (On macOS or Linux you can use a symbolic link instead, as in [Block 5](11e-instructions-skills.qmd).) :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Posit Assistant reads `.agents/skills/` directly, so no copy is needed. ::: ## Step 0: Lock the raw data Everything later depends on the raw file being exactly what the data provider sent. The deny rules from [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) already protect it; here you add a checksumA short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route. and confirm the rules work. **Start:** your workshop repository open, committed and clean, on the `main` branch. (If you are behind and need Block 5's files, switch to `block5-done` from the Git pane's branch menu first.) **1. Record a checksum and commit it.** Run this once, yourself. **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_path <- here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") checksum_path <- here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt") fs::dir_create(here::here("tests", "fixtures")) writeLines(unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path)), checksum_path) ``` ::: Then commit `tests/fixtures/raw_checksum.txt` from the Git pane. **2. Confirm the deny rules are active.** In Claude Code, run `/permissions`. The rules from `.claude/settings.json` should be listed, including the deny ruleA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files. `Edit(/data/raw/**)`. **3. Test the control, do not assume it.** Ask: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Add a comment line to the top of data/raw/voles_raw.csv. ``` It should be refused. Then confirm the file is unchanged. **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_path <- here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") checksum_path <- here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt") identical(unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path)), readLines(checksum_path)) ``` ::: R returns `TRUE`. (The test file in Step 5 checks this too; its other tests skip until the cleaned data exist.) **You are done when** the checksum is committed, the edit was refused and R returned `TRUE`. **If it goes wrong:** if R returns `FALSE`, the raw file changed: open the Git pane, **Revert** `data/raw/voles_raw.csv`, and run the check again. If the agent offers another way to make the edit after the refusal (a shell command, say), decline it. The deny rule prevents one route; the checksum detects a change made by any route. *Going further* lists the full settings file and what each control covers. ## Step 1: Profile the raw data (R, not AI) Profiling is counting, and counting is something you should compute rather than ask a model to estimate. Run the provided script yourself. **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source(here::here("scripts", "00_profile.R")) ``` :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/00_profile.R ---- # Purpose: describe the raw file as entered, before any decision is made. # Every column is read as character so codes such as 9999 or -1 appear # exactly as entered. library(tidyverse) library(here) raw_df <- read_csv( here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()) ) # one row per column: missingness, distinct values, numeric range ---- profile_df <- raw_df |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |> # suppressWarnings: text values become NA here by design mutate(value_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value))) |> summarise( n_rows = n(), n_missing = sum(is.na(value)), n_distinct = n_distinct(value, na.rm = TRUE), n_numeric = sum(!is.na(value_num)), min_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else min(value_num, na.rm = TRUE), max_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else max(value_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = column ) # every distinct label in the categorical columns ---- labels_df <- raw_df |> select(sex, treatment_arm) |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |> count(column, value, sort = TRUE) # identifiers that appear more than once ---- repeated_ids_df <- raw_df |> count(subject_id) |> filter(n > 1) # print in full, and save the profile so it can be opened, pasted or diffed ---- print(profile_df, n = Inf, width = Inf) print(labels_df, n = Inf, width = Inf) print(repeated_ids_df, width = Inf) write_csv(profile_df, here("docs", "profile.csv")) ``` :::
It prints the profile in full and also saves it as `docs/profile.csv`, which you can open with `View(readr::read_csv(here::here("docs", "profile.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE))` (in Positron, the Data Explorer) and paste from in Step 2. Keep it: it is the factual input to the codebook. ## Step 2: Draft the codebook, then audit it The codebook is the data dictionary you wrote for the README on Day 2 ([Fixing it with structure, cleaning and a README](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-fix)), with machine-readable rules added: valid ranges, missing-value codes and label mappings that both the cleaning skill and the validation rules can read. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Draft and audit the codebook (12 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Let an AI draft it from the profile alone.** Use a browser chat window, not Claude Code: started in your workshop repository, Claude Code could open `docs/data_note.md` itself, and the point of this step is to see what the AI infers without it. Paste only the profile output. **Prompt (browser chat):** ```text Here is a profile of a raw data file. Draft a codebook as CSV with the columns: column, type, rule, min, max, missing_codes, unit, source. In the source column, state for every entry whether it comes from the profile or is your assumption. [paste the contents of docs/profile.csv] ``` Save the draft as `docs/codebook.csv` yourself, in the RStudio or Positron editor (*File → New File → Text File*). Avoid Excel: it can change the quoted `rule` fields and the encoding without telling you. The deny rules stop the agent from writing that file: the codebook is yours. **2. Audit the draft.** Before you open `docs/data_note.md`, answer: - Did the draft list `9999` as a missing-value code, or treat it as a large measurement? - Did it notice that `-1` is a code? - Where did its `min` and `max` come from? A range read off the data includes the errors in the data, so it cannot be used to detect them. Valid ranges must come from the biology or the protocol. **3. Correct it against the data provider's note.** Open `docs/data_note.md` and edit the codebook yourself. Every line should be traceable to the note or to a decision you can defend. Where the note does not give a unit (it does not for metabolic rate), write `` rather than a guess: Block 10's README check relies on unknowns staying visible. Commit it. **You are done when** `docs/codebook.csv` is committed, with every rule traceable to the note or to your own decision. **If it goes wrong:** if you are short of time, copy the codebook below into `docs/codebook.csv` and commit it; it is what most groups converge on. :::: :::
``` column,type,rule,min,max,missing_codes,unit,source subject_id,character,"pattern ^V[0-9]{3}$; unique; pad digits to three",,,,,data note sex,character,"allowed M, F; recode male to M, female to F",,,,,data note treatment_arm,character,"allowed Control, Low_dose, High_dose; match case-insensitively",,,,,data note mass_pre_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records) mass_post_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records) metabolic_rate_post,double,,5,30,-1,,data note (range from equipment) ```
## Step 3: Run the validation rules Validation rules are transcribed from the codebook, not from the cleaning script. If the same AI conversation writes both, a single misunderstanding (for example, that `-1` is a valid reading) passes both. The template provides `scripts/functions/validate_voles.R`, written from the codebook by a person. It uses the pointblank package: each line is one rule, and `interrogate()` reports how many rows break it. (pointblank calls the object that holds the rules an "agent"; it has nothing to do with AI agents.) You do not need to write pointblank code today.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/validate_voles.R ---- # Rules transcribed from docs/codebook.csv by a human, not by the agent # that writes the cleaning script. voles_col_types <- function() { readr::cols( subject_id = readr::col_character(), sex = readr::col_character(), treatment_arm = readr::col_character(), mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(), mass_post_g = readr::col_double(), metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double(), .default = readr::col_character() ) } validate_voles <- function(data, label) { data |> pointblank::create_agent(label = label) |> pointblank::col_vals_not_null(columns = c(subject_id, sex, treatment_arm)) |> pointblank::col_vals_regex(columns = subject_id, regex = "^V[0-9]{3}$") |> pointblank::rows_distinct(columns = subject_id) |> pointblank::col_vals_in_set(columns = sex, set = c("M", "F")) |> pointblank::col_vals_in_set( columns = treatment_arm, set = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose") ) |> pointblank::col_vals_between( columns = c(mass_pre_g, mass_post_g), left = 15, right = 60, na_pass = TRUE ) |> pointblank::col_vals_between( columns = metabolic_rate_post, left = 5, right = 30, na_pass = TRUE ) |> pointblank::interrogate() } ``` :::
**Run the rules on the raw data. They should fail.** If raw data pass every rule, either the data are already clean or the rules are too weak, and you should suspect the second. Run the provided script. **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source(here::here("scripts", "02_validate.R")) ``` ::: It prints one line per data set, for example `Raw data (expected to FAIL): 7 of 10 rules fail`, and opens the full report in the Viewer, where you can see which rules fail and how many rows each flags. It also lists any value that could not be read as a number: such a value would become `NA` and slip past the range rules, so the list should be empty. Once the cleaning has run, the same script also validates the clean data, which should pass.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/02_validate.R ---- # Runs the codebook rules on the raw data (expected to FAIL) and, once # 01_clean.R has run, on the clean data (expected to PASS). In an interactive # session the full pointblank report also opens in the Viewer. library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R")) report_validation <- function(validation) { steps <- validation$validation_set n_failed <- sum(!steps$all_passed) cat( validation$label, ": ", if (n_failed == 0) "all rules pass" else paste(n_failed, "of", nrow(steps), "rules fail"), "\n", sep = "" ) if (interactive()) print(validation) invisible(validation) } raw_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) # values that could not be read as numbers become NA and would pass the # range rules, so list them print(problems(raw_df), width = Inf) report_validation(validate_voles(raw_df, "Raw data (expected to FAIL)")) clean_path <- here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv") if (file.exists(clean_path)) { clean_df <- read_csv(clean_path, col_types = voles_col_types()) report_validation(validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data (expected to PASS)")) } ``` :::
Every failure is a problem that the cleaning must resolve or log. :::{.callout-warning} `na_pass = TRUE` lets genuine missing values through. It would also let through a cleaning script that replaced *every* mass with `NA`. Validation alone cannot catch over-cleaning; `tests/test_audit.R` in Step 5 can. ::: ## Step 4: Clean with the skill, plan first The skill holds the procedure; the codebook holds the facts. It sets `disable-model-invocation: true`, so it runs only when you invoke it by name. That is appropriate for a workflow that writes files. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `.agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` markdown --- name: clean-with-codebook description: >- Writes or revises a reproducible R cleaning script that applies a human-authored codebook (docs/codebook.csv) to raw tabular data. Use when asked to clean, recode or prepare raw data in a project that has a codebook. Not for exploratory analysis or modelling. disable-model-invocation: true --- # Clean data against a codebook ## Hard constraints 1. Never modify anything under data/raw/. Read raw files with explicit column types. 2. The codebook is the only source of rules. Do not infer units, ranges, missing-value codes or label mappings that the codebook does not state. 3. Do not edit docs/, scripts/functions/, scripts/02_validate.R, scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R or anything under tests/. If a check fails, report it; never change a check to make it pass. 4. Never drop a row silently. Every excluded row goes in the exclusion log with a reason. 5. Every changed cell goes in the cleaning log. 6. A value outside a codebook range that no codebook rule explains is set to NA, logged with rule "out_of_range_query", and listed in the final report. Never correct it by guessing a unit or decimal error. 7. No imputation. 8. Tidyverse style, native pipe, here::here() for all paths. ## Procedure 1. Present a plan before writing anything: every rule you will apply, the codebook row it comes from, and the order. Wait for the user to confirm. 2. If the data contain a value the codebook does not cover, stop and ask. 3. Write scripts/01_clean.R. It reads docs/codebook.csv when it runs; do not copy rules into the script by hand. Run it in a fresh R session (Rscript scripts/01_clean.R), then run it a second time and confirm the outputs are identical. 4. Run scripts/02_validate.R (raw data should fail, clean data should pass) and every test: Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')". Report both outputs verbatim, including skips. ## Outputs (exact columns) - data/derived/voles_clean.csv: raw_row, then the codebook columns. raw_row is the 1-based row number in the raw file, not counting the header. - data/derived/exclusion_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id (as it appears in the raw file), reason. - data/derived/cleaning_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id, column, old_value, new_value, rule. - rule is one of: missing_code, label_recode, id_format, out_of_range_query. ## Final report Row counts in, out and excluded; every value set to NA for query; any gaps in the codebook you found. ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Plan, review, then execute (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Start:** the codebook committed, the Git pane showing no changed files, and `.claude/skills/clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md` present. **1. Start in plan mode and invoke the skill.** In the Terminal tab, start Claude Code in `plan` mode (`claude --permission-mode plan`, or `Shift+Tab` until the mode shows `plan`), then: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text /clean-with-codebook Clean data/raw/voles_raw.csv using docs/codebook.csv. Start with the plan. ``` :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Switch to plan mode with `/plan`, then invoke the skill with the same prompt. ::: **2. Review the plan before approving it.** Check that: - every rule cites a codebook row; - out-of-range values are set to `NA` and queried, not "corrected"; - no file outside `scripts/01_clean.R` and `data/derived/` will be written; - duplicates are handled by a stated rule, with each exclusion logged. **3. Approve, and keep approving each step.** When Claude Code asks how to proceed, choose **Yes, manually approve edits**, so it still asks before each change (see the [quick reference](11-AI-programming-integrated.qmd#cc-quick-reference)). Read each request, and note every time it stopped to ask you something. A well-behaved agent should stop at least once. While it works, keep the Terminal tab for Claude Code and watch the Git pane: new files should appear only in `scripts/` and `data/derived/` (see [checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work)). **You are done when** `data/derived/` contains `voles_clean.csv`, `cleaning_log.csv` and `exclusion_log.csv`, and the agent has reported the output of `02_validate.R` and of the tests verbatim, as the skill requires. **If it goes wrong:** if the agent stalls, loops or writes outside `scripts/` and `data/derived/`, stop it with `Ctrl+C`, **Revert** its changes in the Git pane, and switch to the `block7-done` branch from the Git pane's branch menu. It contains a working `01_clean.R` and its three outputs, so you can carry on with Step 5. :::: ::: ## Step 5: Check the result **Start:** the three files in `data/derived/` exist, whether the agent wrote them or you switched to `block7-done`. Five checks, each catching something the others cannot. Checks 1 to 3 are the core; if the room is behind, your instructor runs 4 and 5. **1. The tests (the core check).** Two provided test files check everything that can be checked mechanically. Restart R (*Session → Restart R*), then: **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_cleaning.R")) testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_audit.R")) ``` ::: `tests/test_cleaning.R` checks that the raw data are unchanged (the checksum from Step 0), that every raw row is either in the clean data or in the exclusion log with a reason, and that the clean data pass every codebook rule. `tests/test_audit.R` checks the agent's record of its own work, reading the raw data as text, exactly as entered: - every old value in the cleaning log matches the raw file, so the log tells the truth; - every new value in the log is the value in the clean file; - every cell that changed appears in the log, so nothing was altered without a record (the most dangerous outcome in this block); - every rule named in the log is one of the agreed four (`missing_code`, `label_recode`, `id_format`, `out_of_range_query`); - every excluded row's `subject_id` is the one in the raw file; - no more values became `NA` than the codebook's missing-value codes and ranges explain, which catches over-cleaning that validation alone misses. **You are done when** both files pass with no failures. **If it goes wrong:** a failing test names the problem. Ask the agent to fix `01_clean.R`, not the test: the tests and checks are deny-protected, and a check changed to pass proves nothing. If time is short, switch to `block7-done` and run the tests there.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/test_cleaning.R ---- # Block 7: the raw data are untouched, every row is accounted for, and the # clean data pass every codebook rule. library(testthat) testthat::local_edition(3) source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R")) read_chr <- function(...) { readr::read_csv( here::here(...), col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character()) ) } clean_path <- here::here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv") test_that("raw data are unchanged", { checksum_path <- here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt") skip_if_not(file.exists(checksum_path), "Block 7 Step 0 not done yet") recorded <- readLines(checksum_path) current <- unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"))) expect_identical(current, recorded) }) test_that("every raw row is either in the clean data or in the exclusion log", { skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data") raw_df <- read_chr("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") clean_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv") excluded_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "exclusion_log.csv") expect_equal(nrow(raw_df), nrow(clean_df) + nrow(excluded_df)) expect_setequal( c(clean_df$raw_row, excluded_df$raw_row), as.character(seq_len(nrow(raw_df))) ) expect_false(any(is.na(excluded_df$reason) | excluded_df$reason == "")) }) test_that("clean data pass every codebook rule", { skip_if_not(file.exists(clean_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no clean data") clean_df <- readr::read_csv(clean_path, col_types = voles_col_types()) expect_equal(nrow(readr::problems(clean_df)), 0) validation <- validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data") expect_true(pointblank::all_passed(validation)) }) ``` :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/test_audit.R ---- # Block 7: the cleaning log is truthful and complete, and the cleaning did no # more than the codebook allows. Raw values are read as text, exactly as # entered, so a logged old value can be compared character for character. library(testthat) testthat::local_edition(3) log_path <- here::here("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv") allowed_rules <- c("missing_code", "label_recode", "id_format", "out_of_range_query") read_chr <- function(...) { readr::read_csv( here::here(...), col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character()) ) } to_long <- function(data, value_name) { data |> tidyr::pivot_longer(-raw_row, names_to = "column", values_to = value_name) } same <- function(x, y) (is.na(x) & is.na(y)) | (!is.na(x) & !is.na(y) & x == y) audit_inputs <- function() { raw_df <- read_chr("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") |> dplyr::mutate(raw_row = as.character(dplyr::row_number())) clean_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv") log_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv") list( raw = raw_df, clean = clean_df, log = log_df, raw_long = to_long(raw_df, "raw_value"), clean_long = to_long(clean_df, "clean_value") ) } test_that("every logged old value matches the raw file", { skip_if_not(file.exists(log_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no cleaning log") x <- audit_inputs() untruthful <- x$log |> dplyr::left_join(x$raw_long, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |> dplyr::filter(!same(old_value, raw_value)) expect_equal(nrow(untruthful), 0) }) test_that("every logged new value is the value in the clean file", { skip_if_not(file.exists(log_path), "Block 7 not done yet: no cleaning log") x <- audit_inputs() mismatched <- x$log |> ## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. ### The Step 0 controls in full **Line endings.** The template's `.gitattributes` contains this line, so git does not convert line endings, which would change the checksum on Windows: ``` data/raw/** -text ``` **Deny rules.** This is the `.claude/settings.json` in your workshop repository, the same file you read in [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` json { "permissions": { "deny": [ "Edit(/data/raw/**)", "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)", "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)", "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)", "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)", "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)", "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)", "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)", "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)", "Edit(/renv.lock)", "Edit(/.github/**)", "Edit(/.claude/**)", "Edit(/.posit/**)", "Edit(/hooks/**)", "Read(/.Renviron)", "Read(/.env)" ] } } ``` ::: ::: A leading `/` anchors each pattern to the project root. The rules protect specific files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still write `scripts/01_clean.R` and `data/derived/`. Posit Assistant has no documented path rules for file edits; use the guard hook from the *Going further* section of [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) instead. :::{.callout-warning} **What each control covers.** The deny rule blocks the agent's file-editing tools, and shell output redirects such as `> file`. It does not cover R code the agent runs: an R script that writes to `data/raw/` is a different route. The checksum test catches a change made by *any* route, but only after the fact. On the Copilot cloud agent, where you have no local permission file, the checksum test running in CI plus branch protection is your control. Use both where you can: one prevents, the other detects. ::: **Data governance.** A deny rule on editing does not stop data reaching the model provider; see [Block 4](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd). ### Write the validation rules independently Instead of using the provided `validate_voles.R`, you can have the rules written by an AI that has never seen the cleaning code, for example a browser chat window given only the codebook: **Prompt (browser chat):** ```text Using only the codebook below, write an R file containing a function validate_voles(data, label) that builds a pointblank agent with one validation step per codebook rule, and interrogates it. Also write voles_col_types(), returning readr column types for the codebook columns, with character as the default for anything else. [paste docs/codebook.csv] ``` Compare what it writes with the provided version in Step 3. A rule it missed, or a range it took from the data rather than the codebook, is the kind of error the separate conversation is meant to expose. ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
checksum A short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route.
codebook A table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.
deny rule A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.
fresh R session An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.
lockfile The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.
sentinel value A number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for "not recorded" or -1 for "run failed". It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.
